claim: The expansion of the neocortex during primate and human evolution requires the identification of genes that are particularly active in the neural stem and progenitor cells of the developing neocortex.
source: Understanding the molecular basis that underlies the expansion of the neocortex during primate, and notably human, evolution requires the identification of genes that are particularly active in the neural stem and progenitor cells of the developing neocortex.
evidence: This is a statement of the research rationale based on established scientific understanding of neocortical development.

claim: 15 human-specific genes exhibit preferential expression in progenitors of fetal human neocortex.
source: We show that 15 human-specific genes exhibit such expression, and many of them evolved distinct neural progenitor cell-type expression profiles and levels compared to their ancestral paralogs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comprehensive screen described in the manuscript, supported by transcriptome data analysis.

claim: Many human-specific genes evolved distinct neural progenitor cell-type expression profiles and levels compared to their ancestral paralogs.
source: We show that 15 human-specific genes exhibit such expression, and many of them evolved distinct neural progenitor cell-type expression profiles and levels compared to their ancestral paralogs.
evidence: This finding is supported by comparative analysis of expression patterns between human-specific genes and their ancestral paralogs using RNA-Seq data.

claim: NOTCH2NL has the ability to promote basal progenitor proliferation in mice.
source: Functional studies on one such gene, NOTCH2NL, demonstrate its ability to promote basal progenitor proliferation in mice.
evidence: This is supported by in utero electroporation experiments in mouse embryonic neocortex showing increased cycling basal progenitors.

claim: 35 human genes with progenitor-enriched expression have orthologs only in primates.
source: An additional 35 human genes with progenitor-enriched expression are shown to have orthologs only in primates.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and ortholog identification across primate and non-primate genomes.

claim: The expansion of the neocortex in the course of human evolution provides an essential basis for our cognitive abilities.
source: The expansion of the neocortex in the course of human evolution provides an essential basis for our cognitive abilities (Striedter, 2005; Azevedo et al., 2009; Rakic, 2009; Lui et al., 2011; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Buckner and Krienen, 2013; Kaas, 2013; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Dehay et al., 2015; Namba and Huttner, 2017; Sousa et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this relationship.

claim: Neocortical expansion ultimately reflects an increase in the proliferative capacity of cortical neural progenitor cells in the developing human neocortex.
source: This expansion ultimately reflects an increase in the proliferative capacity of the neural stem and progenitor cells in the developing human neocortex (from now on collectively referred to as cortical neural progenitor cells, cNPCs) (Azevedo et al., 2009; Rakic, 2009; Lui et al., 2011; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Bae et al., 2015; Dehay et al., 2015; Namba and Huttner, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on neocortical development.

claim: Neocortical expansion reflects an increase in the duration of the proliferative, neurogenic and gliogenic phases of cortical neural progenitor cells.
source: This expansion ultimately reflects an increase in the proliferative capacity of the neural stem and progenitor cells in the developing human neocortex (from now on collectively referred to as cortical neural progenitor cells, cNPCs) (Azevedo et al., 2009; Rakic, 2009; Lui et al., 2011; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Bae et al., 2015; Dehay et al., 2015; Namba and Huttner, 2017), as well as in the duration of their proliferative, neurogenic and gliogenic phases (Lewitus et al., 2014; Otani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the temporal aspects of neocortical development.

claim: Apical radial glia (aRG) are the primary neuroepithelial cell-derived apical progenitor type.
source: We previously isolated, and determined the transcriptomes of, two major cNPC types from embryonic mouse and fetal human neocortex (Florio et al., 2015), (i) the apical (or ventricular) radial glia (aRG), the primary neuroepithelial cell-derived apical progenitor type (Kriegstein and Götz, 2003; Götz and Huttner, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research characterizing this cell type.

claim: Basal radial glia (bRG) are the key type of basal progenitor implicated in neocortical expansion.
source: We previously isolated, and determined the transcriptomes of, two major cNPC types from embryonic mouse and fetal human neocortex (Florio et al., 2015), (i) the apical (or ventricular) radial glia (aRG), the primary neuroepithelial cell-derived apical progenitor type (Kriegstein and Götz, 2003; Götz and Huttner, 2005), and (ii) the basal (or outer) radial glia (bRG), the key type of basal progenitor implicated in neocortical expansion (Lui et al., 2011; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Betizeau et al., 2013; Borrell and Götz, 2014; Florio and Huttner, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on bRG and neocortical expansion.

claim: 263 protein-coding human genes are much more highly expressed in human bRG and aRG than in a neuron-enriched fraction.
source: This led to the identification of 263 protein-coding human genes that are much more highly expressed in human bRG and aRG than in a neuron-enriched fraction (Florio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior transcriptome analysis by the authors.

claim: Of the 263 genes highly expressed in human bRG and aRG, 207 genes have orthologs in the mouse genome but are not expressed in mouse cNPCs.
source: Of these, 207 genes have orthologs in the mouse genome but are not expressed in mouse cNPCs, whereas 56 genes lack mouse orthologs.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis between human and mouse transcriptomes from prior work.

claim: 56 of the 263 genes highly expressed in human bRG and aRG lack mouse orthologs.
source: Of these, 207 genes have orthologs in the mouse genome but are not expressed in mouse cNPCs, whereas 56 genes lack mouse orthologs.
evidence: This is based on ortholog analysis from prior work.

claim: ARHGAP11B is a human-specific gene.
source: Among the latter, the gene with the highest specificity of expression in bRG and aRG was found to be ARHGAP11B, a human-specific gene (Riley et al., 2002; Sudmant et al., 2010; Antonacci et al., 2014; Dennis et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing the human-specific nature of this gene.

claim: ARHGAP11B is capable of basal progenitor amplification in embryonic mouse neocortex.
source: Among the latter, the gene with the highest specificity of expression in bRG and aRG was found to be ARHGAP11B, a human-specific gene (Riley et al., 2002; Sudmant et al., 2010; Antonacci et al., 2014; Dennis et al., 2017) that we showed to be capable of basal progenitor amplification in embryonic mouse neocortex, which likely contributed to the evolutionary expansion of the human neocortex (Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on functional studies by the authors in prior work.

claim: ARHGAP11B likely contributed to the evolutionary expansion of the human neocortex.
source: Among the latter, the gene with the highest specificity of expression in bRG and aRG was found to be ARHGAP11B, a human-specific gene (Riley et al., 2002; Sudmant et al., 2010; Antonacci et al., 2014; Dennis et al., 2017) that we showed to be capable of basal progenitor amplification in embryonic mouse neocortex, which likely contributed to the evolutionary expansion of the human neocortex (Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional properties of ARHGAP11B demonstrated in prior work.

claim: Five published transcriptome datasets from fetal human neocortical tissue and cell populations were screened for protein-coding genes showing higher levels of mRNA expression in germinal zones and cNPC types than in non-proliferative zones and neurons.
source: The indicated five published transcriptome datasets from fetal human neocortical tissue (Fietz et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2014) and cell populations (Florio et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2015; Pollen et al., 2015), were screened for protein-coding genes showing higher levels of mRNA expression in the indicated germinal zones and cNPC types than in the non-proliferative zones and neurons.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Fietz et al. dataset yielded 2780 genes more highly expressed in VZ, iSVZ, and/or oSVZ than CP.
source: This yielded 2780 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the Fietz dataset as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Miller et al. dataset yielded 3802 genes with positive laminar correlation with VZ, iSVZ or oSVZ.
source: This yielded 3802 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the Miller dataset as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Florio et al. dataset yielded 2030 genes more highly expressed in aRG and/or bRG than in neurons.
source: This yielded 2030 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the Florio dataset as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Pollen et al. dataset yielded 4391 genes positively correlated with radial glial cells and/or bIPs and negatively correlated with neurons.
source: This yielded 4391 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the Pollen dataset as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Johnson et al. dataset yielded 1617 genes more highly expressed in aRG and/or bRG than in the cell population enriched in bIPs and neurons.
source: This yielded 1617 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the Johnson dataset as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pairwise comparison of cNPC-enriched gene sets revealed a substantial overlap between datasets, ranging from 32% to 60%.
source: Pairwise comparison of these cNPC-enriched gene sets revealed a substantial overlap between datasets, ranging from 32% (Florio-Pollen) to 60% (Fietz-Miller) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of the gene sets as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 562 protein-coding genes were found in all five gene sets.
source: This was the case for 562 genes (Figure 1D, yellow).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 1D.

claim: 3458 human genes with preferential expression in cNPCs were found in at least two gene sets.
source: Together this yielded a catalogue of 3458 human genes with preferential expression in cNPCs in at least two gene sets (from here on referred to as cNPC-enriched genes) (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the main result from the intersection of the five gene sets as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The 3458 cNPC-enriched genes include many canonical markers of cNPCs and known molecular players involved in radial glia function, intermediate progenitor function, cell proliferation, Notch signaling, and extracellular matrix and growth factor signaling.
source: These 3458 genes included many canonical markers of cNPCs and known molecular players involved in (i) function of radial glia (e.g. FABP7, GFAP, NES, VIM, PROM (Taverna et al., 2014), PAX6 (Osumi et al., 2008; Walcher et al., 2013), SOX2 (Lui et al., 2011), HOPX (Pollen et al., 2015)) and intermediate progenitors (e.g. EOMES (Englund et al., 2005), NEUROG1/2 (Fode et al., 2000; Schuurmans et al., 2004)), (ii) cell proliferation (e.g. MKI67, PCNA), (iii) Notch signaling (e.g. DLL1, HES1, HES5, NOTCH1, NOTCH3 (Kageyama et al., 2009; Imayoshi et al., 2013)), and (iv) extracellular matrix and growth factor signaling (e.g. EGF, FGFR2, FGFR3 (Vaccarino et al., 1999), ITGAV (Stenzel et al., 2014), TGFB1, TNC (von Holst et al., 2007)) (listed in Figure 1E).
evidence: This validates the gene set by showing it contains known cNPC markers, supported by multiple citations.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis revealed that for the category Biological Process, 'cell cycle phase and mitotic cell cycle phase', 'mitotic prometaphase' and 'M phase and mitotic M phase' were the three most enriched terms.
source: This revealed that for the category Biological Process the GO terms 'cell cycle phase and mitotic cell cycle phase', 'mitotic prometaphase' and 'M phase and mitotic M phase' were the three most enriched ones
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of the 3458 cNPC-enriched genes as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis revealed that for the category Cellular Component, 'chromosome centromeric region', 'condensed chromosome centromeric region' and 'kinetochore' were the three most enriched terms.
source: for the category Cellular Component the GO terms 'chromosome centromeric region', 'condensed chromosome centromeric region' and 'kinetochore' were the three most enriched ones (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of the 3458 cNPC-enriched genes as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The cNPC-enriched genes preferentially encode proteins involved in cell division, including core components of the mitotic machinery.
source: This underscored that the cNPC-enriched genes identified here preferentially encode proteins involved in cell division, including core components of the mitotic machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GO term enrichment analysis results.

claim: 77 of the 3458 human cNPC-enriched genes were candidates to be primate-specific after excluding genes with annotated one-to-one orthologs in non-primate species.
source: This yielded 77 genes that were candidates to be primate-specific.
evidence: This is based on ortholog analysis as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 50 genes were considered to be truly primate-specific after manual inspection of genomic alignments and gene annotations.
source: The remaining 50 genes were considered to be truly primate-specific (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on detailed genomic analysis as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 25 of the 50 primate-specific genes predate the ape (Hominoidea) ancestor.
source: First, we found that 25 of these 50 genes predate the ape (Hominoidea) ancestor
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 14 of the 25 primate-specific genes that predate the ape ancestor encode zinc finger proteins.
source: First, we found that 25 of these 50 genes predate the ape (Hominoidea) ancestor and that 14 of these 25 genes encode zinc finger proteins (Figure 2A, Table 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and functional domain analysis as shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: 15 of the 50 primate-specific genes are only present in the human genome and arose after the split from the chimpanzee lineage.
source: Remarkably, 15 of the remaining 25 genes that postdate the ape ancestor are only present in the human genome, and thus arose (or evolved to their present state) in the human lineage after its split from the lineage leading to the chimpanzee (Figure 2A, Table 1 and Supplementary file 3) (~5–7 Mya, (Brunet et al., 2002; Vignaud et al., 2002; Brunet et al., 2005)).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis as shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: The human-chimpanzee lineage split occurred approximately 5-7 million years ago.
source: Remarkably, 15 of the remaining 25 genes that postdate the ape ancestor are only present in the human genome, and thus arose (or evolved to their present state) in the human lineage after its split from the lineage leading to the chimpanzee (Figure 2A, Table 1 and Supplementary file 3) (~5–7 Mya, (Brunet et al., 2002; Vignaud et al., 2002; Brunet et al., 2005)).
evidence: This is based on cited paleontological evidence.

claim: ARHGAP11B was present in the archaic genomes of Neandertals and Denisovans.
source: These 15 human-specific genes include ARHGAP11B, a gene that we reported previously to promote cNPC proliferation and neocortex expansion (Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016) and that was also present in the archaic genomes of Neandertals and Denisovans (Sudmant et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2012; Antonacci et al., 2014; Prüfer et al., 2014; Florio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on analysis of archaic human genomes as cited.

claim: 13 of the 14 remaining human-specific genes (besides ARHGAP11B) existed in the genomes of Neandertals and Denisovans and arose before the split of modern humans from Neandertals/Denisovans approximately 500,000 years ago.
source: Similar to ARHGAP11B, 13 of the remaining 14 human-specific genes existed also in the genomes of Neandertals and Denisovans (Sudmant et al., 2010; Dennis et al., 2017) and present data (see Table 1) and thus arose before the split of the lineages leading to modern humans vs. Neandertals/Denisovans ~500,000 years ago (Meyer et al., 2012; Prüfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of archaic human genomes and phylogenetic dating as cited.

claim: SMN2 is the only one of the 15 human-specific genes that arose in the lineage leading to modern humans after its divergence from Neandertals and Denisovans.
source: The only one of the 15 human-specific genes that has been reported to have arisen in the lineage leading to modern humans after its divergence from the lineage leading to Neandertals and Denisovans is SMN2 (Dennis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited research on SMN2 evolution.

claim: SMN2 can alleviate spinal muscular atrophy, a neurological disease caused by mutations of SMN1.
source: The SMN2 gene can alleviate spinal muscular atrophy, a neurological disease caused by mutations of SMN1 (the ancestral paralog of SMN2) (Parsons et al., 1996; Lorson et al., 1999; Watihayati et al., 2009)
evidence: This is based on cited clinical and genetic research.

claim: SMN2 can be regarded as an inefficient SMN1 back-up specific to modern humans.
source: The SMN2 gene can alleviate spinal muscular atrophy, a neurological disease caused by mutations of SMN1 (the ancestral paralog of SMN2) (Parsons et al., 1996; Lorson et al., 1999; Watihayati et al., 2009), and thus can be regarded as an, albeit inefficient, SMN1 back-up specific to modern humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional relationship between SMN2 and SMN1 and the evolutionary timing of SMN2 emergence.

claim: There was a disproportionately high rate of appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes in the branch leading to Catarrhini and the branch leading to human.
source: This revealed a disproportionately high rate of appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes in two of the branches, the branch that leads to Catarrhini (branch 6) and the branch that leads to human (branch 1) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene emergence rates relative to neutral substitution rates as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MICA arose by duplication of the MICB gene in the Catarrhini ancestor.
source: MICA is a paradigmatic example of a gene arising by gene duplication (Bailey et al., 2002; Eichler et al., 2004; Fortna et al., 2004; Hurles, 2004), a well-known driving force of genome evolution (Lynch and Conery, 2000). MICA arose by duplication of the MICB gene, and this event occurred in the Catarrhini ancestor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and cited research on gene duplication as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gene duplication is a well-known driving force of genome evolution.
source: MICA is a paradigmatic example of a gene arising by gene duplication (Bailey et al., 2002; Eichler et al., 2004; Fortna et al., 2004; Hurles, 2004), a well-known driving force of genome evolution (Lynch and Conery, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology supported by citations.

claim: KIF4B evolved in the Simiiformes ancestor by retroposition of KIF4A.
source: In fact, KIF4B is the only member of the kinesin superfamily among the 50 primate-specific genes. KIF4B evolved in the Simiiformes ancestor (Figure 2A) by retroposition of KIF4A, a gene with a near-ubiquitous occurrence in the animal kingdom (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and cited research as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KIF4A has a near-ubiquitous occurrence in the animal kingdom.
source: KIF4B evolved in the Simiiformes ancestor (Figure 2A) by retroposition of KIF4A, a gene with a near-ubiquitous occurrence in the animal kingdom (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited research on kinesin evolution.

claim: Retroposition of KIF4A involved reverse transcription of a spliced KIF4A mRNA followed by insertion of the DNA into the genome as an intronless copy.
source: This retroposition involved the reverse transcription of a spliced KIF4A mRNA followed by insertion of the DNA into the genome as an intronless copy of KIF4A.
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism of retroposition based on genomic analysis.

claim: PTTG2 arose by retroposition of a reverse transcribed spliced mRNA of PTTG1.
source: Similar to KIF4B, the primate-specific gene PTTG2 arose by retroposition of a reverse transcribed spliced mRNA of PTTG1, a gene encompassing five protein-coding exons that are conserved in reptiles, birds and mammals.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PTTG1 encompasses five protein-coding exons that are conserved in reptiles, birds and mammals.
source: Similar to KIF4B, the primate-specific gene PTTG2 arose by retroposition of a reverse transcribed spliced mRNA of PTTG1, a gene encompassing five protein-coding exons that are conserved in reptiles, birds and mammals.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The intronless protein-coding PTTG2 inserted in sense direction into intron 2 of the TBC1D1 gene.
source: However, while KIF4B inserted into an intergenic locus (that however allowed its transcription), the intronless protein-coding PTTG2 inserted in sense direction into intron 2 of the TBC1D1 gene (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TBC1D1 encodes a Rab-GTPase activating protein.
source: However, while KIF4B inserted into an intergenic locus (that however allowed its transcription), the intronless protein-coding PTTG2 inserted in sense direction into intron 2 of the TBC1D1 gene (Figure 3A), which encodes a Rab-GTPase activating protein (Roach et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on cited research on TBC1D1 function.

claim: The PTTG2 retroposition event occurred in the Simiiform ancestor.
source: Remarkably, whereas the PTTG2 retroposition event already occurred in the Simiiform ancestor, the PTTG2 gene underwent two principally different lines of evolution after retroposition.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In all non-Hominoidea Simiiformes, PTTG2 accumulated frameshifting deletions and translational stop codon mutations that cause premature termination of the open-reading frame.
source: In all non-Hominoidea Simiiformes (see Figure 2A), consistent with neutral evolution, PTTG2 accumulated frameshifting deletions and translational stop codon mutations that cause a premature termination of the open-reading frame (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Hominoidea, the PTTG2 reading frame remained open.
source: In contrast, in Hominoidea (apes and humans, see Figure 2A), the PTTG2 reading frame remained open, with one noticeable change.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A 1 bp insertion near the 3' end of the PTTG2 open-reading frame causes a shift in the reading frame, resulting in a new 13-amino acid-long C-terminal sequence of PTTG2 in great apes.
source: This is a 1 bp insertion (T, see Figure 3A) near the 3' end of the PTTG2 open-reading frame that causes a shift in the reading frame, resulting in a new 13-amino acid-long C-terminal sequence of PTTG2 in great apes (including human) (as opposed to 24 amino acids in PTTG1) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The PTTG2-specific C-terminal sequence in great apes lacks the cluster of acidic residues found in the C-terminal sequence of PTTG1.
source: This PTTG2-specific sequence lacks the cluster of acidic residues found in the C-terminal sequence of PTTG1.
evidence: This is based on protein sequence comparison.

claim: In gibbon, the PTTG2 gene carries a 22 bp deletion in addition to the 1 bp T insertion, causing another shift in the reading frame that results in the replacement of the C-terminal 25 amino acids of the PTTG2 of great apes by an 18-amino acid-long sequence.
source: In the case of the gibbon, however, the PTTG2 gene carries (in addition to the 1 bp T insertion) a 22 bp deletion a few nucleotides 5' to this insertion. This causes yet another shift in the reading frame that results in the replacement of the C-terminal 25 amino acids of the PTTG2 of great apes (including human) by an 18-amino acid-long sequence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 12 of the 15 human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes arose by duplications of entire genes.
source: Twelve of them arose by duplications of entire genes (Bailey et al., 2002; Eichler et al., 2004; Fortna et al., 2004; Hurles, 2004) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NOTCH2NL arose from a duplication that included the genes NBPF7, ADAM30, and NOTCH2.
source: A special case, illustrating possible evolutionary trajectories after gene duplication, is the human-specific cNPC-enriched NOTCH2NL gene (Figure 4A). It arose from a duplication that included the genes NBPF7, ADAM30, and NOTCH2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After the gene duplication event that gave rise to NOTCH2NL, a deletion occurred that removed the duplicated ADAM30 gene and a large portion of the duplicated NOTCH2 gene.
source: After the gene duplication event, a deletion occurred that removed the duplicated ADAM30 gene and a large portion of the duplicated NOTCH2 gene.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deletion that occurred after NOTCH2NL duplication removed most of the sequence giving rise to the two long NOTCH2 splice variants.
source: This portion included most of the sequence giving rise to the two long NOTCH2 splice variants (ENST00000256646 and ENST00000579475).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The remaining duplicated NOTCH2 gene sequence (NOTCH2NL) gives rise to a short splice variant that encodes only a short segment of the NOTCH2 ectodomain.
source: The remaining duplicated NOTCH2 gene sequence (the NOTCH2NL gene) gives rise to a short splice variant (ENST00000602566) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) that encodes only a short segment of the NOTCH2 ectodomain.
evidence: This is based on genomic and transcript analysis as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARHGAP11B arose by partial gene duplication.
source: One gene, ARHGAP11B, arose by a partial gene duplication (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The evolution of ARHGAP11B has been analyzed previously.
source: Its evolution has been analyzed previously (Riley et al., 2002; Antonacci et al., 2014; Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016; Dennis et al., 2017; Dougherty et al., 2017).
evidence: This refers to prior published work on ARHGAP11B evolution.

claim: An exon of ZNF98 inserted into the ZNF492 locus in humans, yielding a chimeric human-specific protein containing the repressor domain of ZNF492 and the DNA binding domain of ZNF98.
source: The ZNF492 gene as such exists in the genomes of all non-human great apes. In the case of human, however, an exon of another zinc finger protein-encoding gene, ZNF98, inserted into the ZNF492 locus, yielding a chimeric human-specific protein containing the repressor domain of ZNF492 and the DNA binding domain of ZNF98 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FAM182B exists in human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla, but in bonobo and gorilla a stop codon terminates the potential open-reading frame soon after the initiator methionine.
source: The FAM182B gene as such exists not only in human but also in chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla. However, in bonobo and gorilla, a stop codon terminates the potential open-reading frame soon after the initiator methionine
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In human FAM182B, a single T→G substitution replaces a premature stop codon with a sense codon to yield a 152-amino acid-long protein.
source: whereas in human a single T–>G substitution replaces this premature stop with a sense codon to yield a 152-amino acid-long protein (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In chimpanzee FAM182B, the T of the TAG stop codon is deleted, resulting in a reading frame shift that predicts a shorter, 52-amino acid-long polypeptide.
source: In chimpanzee, the T of the TAG stop codon is deleted, which we confirmed by genomic PCR (data not shown), resulting in a reading frame shift that predicts a shorter, 52-amino acid-long polypeptide.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic sequence analysis and confirmed by genomic PCR.

claim: The human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes evolved mainly by entire or partial gene duplications.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes evolved mainly by entire or partial gene duplications.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the evolutionary mechanisms of the 15 human-specific genes.

claim: Genomic qPCR validated the human-specific nature of ARHGAP11B by showing a two-fold increase of the human PCR product compared to bonobo and chimpanzee.
source: Using the bonobo gene as the standard, this resulted in a two-fold increase of the human PCR product compared to the bonobo and chimpanzee, confirming that ARHGAP11B is indeed a human-specific gene duplication (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is based on genomic qPCR data as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated four human copies of FAM72 (the ancestral FAM72A plus three human-specific paralogs FAM72B/C/D) compared to one copy in chimpanzee and bonobo.
source: For the other five human-specific cNPC-enriched genes (FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) and for the human-specific gene GTF2H2B for which primers could be designed, genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated four human copies of FAM72 (i.e. the ancestral FAM72A plus its three human-specific paralogs FAM72B/C/D), three human copies of GTF2H2 (i.e. the ancestral GTF2H2 and the two human-specific paralogs GTF2H2B/C) and two human copies of SMN (i.e. ancestral SMN1 and its human-specific paralog SMN2) (Figure 4E), compared to only one copy in both chimpanzee and bonobo.
evidence: This is based on genomic qPCR data as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated three human copies of GTF2H2 (the ancestral GTF2H2 and two human-specific paralogs GTF2H2B/C) compared to one copy in chimpanzee and bonobo.
source: For the other five human-specific cNPC-enriched genes (FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) and for the human-specific gene GTF2H2B for which primers could be designed, genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated four human copies of FAM72 (i.e. the ancestral FAM72A plus its three human-specific paralogs FAM72B/C/D), three human copies of GTF2H2 (i.e. the ancestral GTF2H2 and the two human-specific paralogs GTF2H2B/C) and two human copies of SMN (i.e. ancestral SMN1 and its human-specific paralog SMN2) (Figure 4E), compared to only one copy in both chimpanzee and bonobo.
evidence: This is based on genomic qPCR data as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated two human copies of SMN (ancestral SMN1 and human-specific paralog SMN2) compared to one copy in chimpanzee and bonobo.
source: For the other five human-specific cNPC-enriched genes (FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) and for the human-specific gene GTF2H2B for which primers could be designed, genomic qPCR resulted in an estimated four human copies of FAM72 (i.e. the ancestral FAM72A plus its three human-specific paralogs FAM72B/C/D), three human copies of GTF2H2 (i.e. the ancestral GTF2H2 and the two human-specific paralogs GTF2H2B/C) and two human copies of SMN (i.e. ancestral SMN1 and its human-specific paralog SMN2) (Figure 4E), compared to only one copy in both chimpanzee and bonobo.
evidence: This is based on genomic qPCR data as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The percentage of DNA sequence reads of the PCR amplicons that aligned to the targeted genomic sequences ranged from 97.2 to 99.8, indicating that the PCR reactions were highly specific.
source: The percentage of the DNA sequence reads of the PCR amplicons that aligned to the targeted genomic sequences ranged from 97.2 to 99.8, indicating that the PCR reactions were highly specific (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequencing validation of genomic qPCR amplicons as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The absolute number of DNA sequence reads that aligned to the respective genomic sequence corresponded to the gene copy numbers as determined by genomic qPCR.
source: Moreover, the absolute number of DNA sequence reads that aligned to the respective genomic sequence of either one of the seven human-specific genes or its ancestral paralog (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) corresponded to the gene copy numbers as determined by the genomic qPCR (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on comparison of sequencing data with qPCR data as shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ARHGAP11B mRNA expression is detected in all three germinal zones (VZ, iSVZ and oSVZ) but not in the CP.
source: In the case of ARHGAP11B, we used a specific Locked Nucleic Acid (LNA) probe, which enabled us to distinguish the mRNA of ARHGAP11B from that of ARHGAP11A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). mRNA expression was detected in all three germinal zones (VZ, iSVZ and oSVZ) but not in the CP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NOTCH2NL expression is essentially restricted to the VZ.
source: Expression of NOTCH2NL was essentially restricted to the VZ (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DHRS4L2 and ZNF492 are expressed in all three germinal zones and the CP, with stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP.
source: DHRS4L2 and ZNF492 were found to be expressed in all three germinal zones and the CP, with a stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP (Figure 5F,I).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5F and 5I.

claim: GTF2H2C mRNA expression is detected in the three germinal zones and the CP, with stronger staining in the VZ, iSVZ and CP than in the oSVZ.
source: GTF2H2C mRNA expression was also detected in the three germinal zones and the CP, but with stronger staining in the VZ, iSVZ and CP than in the oSVZ (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FAM182B mRNA expression is stronger in the VZ and CP than in the iSVZ and oSVZ.
source: Finally, in the case of FAM182B, mRNA expression was stronger in the VZ and CP than in the iSVZ and oSVZ (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5J.

claim: ARHGAP11A mRNA expression shows a striking difference to ARHGAP11B, being detected in the IZ and to some extent the CP in addition to the germinal zones.
source: The mRNA expression pattern of the ancestral paralog ARHGAP11A (Figure 5A) showed a striking difference to that of the human-specific gene ARHGAP11B (Figure 5A,B). Whereas ARHGAP11B expression was largely restricted to the three germinal zones (Figure 5B), ARHGAP11A expression was also detected in the IZ and to some extent the CP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: ARHGAP11A shows a specific ISH signal at the basal surface of the CP, which likely reflects concentration of ARHGAP11A mRNA in the basal end-feet of radial glial cells.
source: Of note, ARHGAP11A, in contrast to ARHGAP11B, showed a specific ISH signal at the basal surface of the CP, which likely reflects concentration of ARHGAP11A mRNA in the basal end-feet of radial glial cells (Figure 5A,B), a subcellular site at which certain mRNAs can be concentrated (Tsunekawa et al., 2012; Pilaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5A and 5B, with inference supported by citations.

claim: mRNA localization of ancestral NOTCH2 is virtually identical to the expression pattern of human-specific NOTCH2NL.
source: In contrast to ARHGAP11A/B, mRNA localization of ancestral NOTCH2 (Figure 5C) was virtually identical to the expression pattern of human-specific NOTCH2NL described above (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The combined mRNA expression patterns of DHRS4/L1/L2 are similar to that of DHRS4L2, with stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP.
source: The combined mRNA expression patterns of DHRS4/L1/L2 were similar to that of DHRS4L2, and the combined mRNA expression patterns of GTF2H2/B/C were similar to that of GTF2H2C, with stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP in both cases (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The combined mRNA expression patterns of GTF2H2/B/C are similar to that of GTF2H2C, with stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP.
source: The combined mRNA expression patterns of DHRS4/L1/L2 were similar to that of DHRS4L2, and the combined mRNA expression patterns of GTF2H2/B/C were similar to that of GTF2H2C, with stronger signal in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP in both cases (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: ANKRD20A1-4 expression is essentially confined to the VZ.
source: In the case of ANKRD20A1-4 (which included the cNPC-enriched human-specific genes ANKRD20A2 and ANKRD20A4, ancestral ANKRD20A1, and yet another paralog, ANKRD20A3), expression was essentially confined to the VZ (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5K.

claim: CBWD1-6 mRNA expression is stronger in the VZ and CP than iSVZ and oSVZ.
source: In the case of CBWD1-6 (which included the cNPC-enriched human-specific gene CBWD6, ancestral CBWD1, and CBWD2-5), mRNA expression was stronger in the VZ and CP than iSVZ and oSVZ (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5L.

claim: FAM72A-D mRNA expression is stronger in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP.
source: In the case of FAM72A-D (which included the cNPC-enriched human-specific genes FAM72B, FAM72C, and FAM72D and ancestral FAM72A), mRNA expression was stronger in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5M.

claim: SMN1-2 mRNA expression is stronger in the VZ and iSVZ than in the oSVZ and CP.
source: A similar expression pattern was found for SMN1-2 (which included the cNPC-enriched human-specific gene SMN2 and ancestral SMN1) (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 5N.

claim: mRNA expression for PTTG1/2 is robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
source: mRNA expression for PTTG1/2 (Figure 6A), MICA/B (Figure 6B) and KIF4A/B (Figure 6C) was robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: mRNA expression for MICA/B is robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
source: mRNA expression for PTTG1/2 (Figure 6A), MICA/B (Figure 6B) and KIF4A/B (Figure 6C) was robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: mRNA expression for KIF4A/B is robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
source: mRNA expression for PTTG1/2 (Figure 6A), MICA/B (Figure 6B) and KIF4A/B (Figure 6C) was robust in the human VZ and iSVZ, relatively low in the oSVZ, and moderate in the CP.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: With the exception of NOTCH2NL, the majority of human-specific genes showed markedly different total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog.
source: We first focused on changes in total mRNA levels between the human-specific genes and their ancestral paralogs. With the exception of NOTCH2NL, for which the total mRNA levels in aRG, bRG, and N were in the same range as the corresponding ancestral paralog, we found that the majority of the human-specific genes showed markedly different total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog, which were either reduced (ARHGAP11B, CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) or increased (ANKRD20A2, ANKRD20A4, DHRS4L2, ZNF492) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ARHGAP11B, CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, and SMN2 showed reduced total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog.
source: With the exception of NOTCH2NL, for which the total mRNA levels in aRG, bRG, and N were in the same range as the corresponding ancestral paralog, we found that the majority of the human-specific genes showed markedly different total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog, which were either reduced (ARHGAP11B, CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) or increased (ANKRD20A2, ANKRD20A4, DHRS4L2, ZNF492) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ANKRD20A2, ANKRD20A4, DHRS4L2, and ZNF492 showed increased total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog.
source: With the exception of NOTCH2NL, for which the total mRNA levels in aRG, bRG, and N were in the same range as the corresponding ancestral paralog, we found that the majority of the human-specific genes showed markedly different total mRNA expression levels compared to their ancestral paralog, which were either reduced (ARHGAP11B, CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, GTF2H2C, SMN2) or increased (ANKRD20A2, ANKRD20A4, DHRS4L2, ZNF492) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: For five human-specific genes (CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, and NOTCH2NL), the pattern of mRNA levels in aRG, bRG, and N was similar to that of the respective ancestral paralog.
source: For five of the human-specific genes (CBWD6, FAM72B/C/D, and NOTCH2NL), the pattern of mRNA levels in these three cell populations was similar to that of the respective ancestral paralog (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ZNF492 expression is lower in bRG than aRG, in contrast to ancestral ZNF98 expression.
source: For instance, ZNF492 expression is lower in bRG than aRG, in contrast to what is observed for ancestral ZNF98 expression.
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ARHGAP11B, DHRS4L2, GTF2H2C, and SMN2 expression is higher in bRG than aRG, in contrast to what is observed for the respective ancestral paralog.
source: Vice versa, ARHGAP11B, DHRS4L2, GTF2H2C, and SMN2 expression is higher in bRG than aRG, in contrast to what is observed for the respective ancestral paralog.
evidence: This is based on Kallisto analysis of RNA-Seq data as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The increase in ARHGAP11B mRNA level in bRG compared to aRG is consistent with the previously reported function of this gene in basal progenitor amplification.
source: Of note, the increase in the ARHGAP11B mRNA level in bRG as compared to aRG is consistent with the previously reported function of this gene in basal progenitor amplification (Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference connecting expression data with prior functional studies.

claim: After duplication, the expression pattern of most of the new human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes evolved differences in both the levels and cell-type specificity of their mRNAs compared to their respective ancestral paralog.
source: In summary, these analyses show that after duplication, the expression pattern of most of the resulting new, human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes evolved differences in both the levels and cell-type specificity of their mRNAs compared to their respective ancestral paralog.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the expression analysis data.

claim: In utero electroporation of NOTCH2NL in E13.5 mouse embryos revealed an increase in cycling basal progenitors in the SVZ and IZ, but not in apical progenitors in the VZ, 48 hr after electroporation.
source: Analysis of the progeny of the targeted aRG by immunofluorescence for PCNA and Ki67, two markers of cycling cells, 48 hr after NOTCH2NL electroporation revealed an increase in cycling basal progenitors in the SVZ and IZ, but not in apical progenitors in the VZ (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation experiments and immunofluorescence analysis as shown in Figure 9A-D.

claim: The increase in cycling basal progenitors upon NOTCH2NL expression involved bIPs expressing Tbr2, rather than bRG expressing Sox2.
source: This increase involved bIPs expressing Tbr2 (Figure 9F,G), rather than bRG expressing Sox2 (Figure 9H,I).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis as shown in Figure 9F-I.

claim: Concomitant with the increase in cycling basal progenitors, there was a decrease in cell cycle exit in the SVZ upon NOTCH2NL expression.
source: Concomitant with this increase, we observed a decrease in cell cycle exit in the SVZ, as indicated by the decrease in Ki67 expression in the progeny of BrdU-labeled cells derived from the targeted aRG (Figure 9C,E).
evidence: This is based on BrdU labeling and immunofluorescence analysis as shown in Figure 9C and 9E.

claim: Analysis of mitotic cNPCs using phosphohistone H3 immunofluorescence showed an increase in abventricular, but not ventricular, mitoses upon NOTCH2NL expression.
source: These data were further corroborated by analysis of mitotic cNPCs using phosphohistone H3 immunofluorescence, which showed an increase in abventricular, but not ventricular, mitoses (Figure 9J,K).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis as shown in Figure 9J and 9K.

claim: Forced expression of the human-specific NOTCH2NL gene in mouse embryonic neocortex promotes basal progenitor proliferation.
source: Thus, forced expression of the human-specific NOTCH2NL gene in mouse embryonic neocortex promotes basal progenitor proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in utero electroporation experiments.

claim: Different mechanisms contributed to the origin of human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes.
source: As to the emergence of these genes during primate evolution, two aspects of our findings deserve comment. First, different mechanisms contributed to the origin of human-specific cNPC-enriched protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the evolutionary analysis of the genes.

claim: Entire or partial gene duplications gave rise to the vast majority of human-specific cNPC-enriched genes.
source: While entire or partial gene duplications gave rise to the vast majority of these genes, consistent with previous results (Bailey et al., 2002; Eichler et al., 2004; Fortna et al., 2004; Hurles, 2004)
evidence: This is based on the evolutionary analysis and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Exon duplications can give rise to chimeric genes, as observed for ZNF492.
source: we found that exon duplications can give rise to chimeric genes, as observed for ZNF492
evidence: This is based on the genomic analysis of ZNF492.

claim: The removal of a translational stop codon can create a new open reading frame, as observed for FAM182B.
source: and that the removal of a translational stop codon can create a new open reading frame, as observed for FAM182B.
evidence: This is based on the genomic analysis of FAM182B.

claim: Among primate- but not human-specific genes, two genes with functions likely relevant for cell proliferation (KIF4B, PTTG2) arose by retroposition of a reverse transcribed spliced mRNA.
source: Among the primate- but not human-specific genes, two genes with functions that are likely relevant for cell proliferation (KIF4B, PTTG2; (Brosius, 1991; Long et al., 2003; Marques et al., 2005)) arose by retroposition of a reverse transcribed spliced mRNA, highlighting another mechanism for the emergence of new genes.
evidence: This is based on the evolutionary analysis of KIF4B and PTTG2.

claim: PTTG2 was inactivated during the evolution of non-Hominoidea Simiiformes but remained intact during the evolution of Hominoidea.
source: Here, PTTG2 is a particularly interesting case, since it was inactivated during the evolution of non-Hominoidea Simiiformes but remained intact during the evolution of Hominoidea.
evidence: This is based on the comparative genomic analysis of PTTG2 across primate species.

claim: PTTG2 may exert a role in the development of the neocortex of apes and human but not of New-World and Old-World monkeys.
source: This raises the possibility that PTTG2 may exert a role in the development of the neocortex of apes and human but not of New-World and Old-World monkeys.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evolutionary pattern of PTTG2.

claim: Of the 50 primate-specific human genes, 30% are human-specific and 34% arose in the Catarrhini ancestor.
source: Second, of the 50 primate-specific human genes, 15 (30%) are human-specific and 17 (34%) arose in the Catarrhini ancestor.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis of the 50 primate-specific genes.

claim: The percentages of human-specific and Catarrhini-specific genes are higher than expected from a constant rate of gene emergence on the phylogenetic branches leading from the primate ancestor to human.
source: These percentages are higher than expected from a constant rate of gene emergence on the phylogenetic branches leading from the primate ancestor to human.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of observed gene emergence rates with expected rates under a constant model.

claim: The increased appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes in the branch leading to Catarrhini may be related to the concomitant increase in gyrencephaly.
source: With regard to the branch leading to Catarrhini, one may speculate whether the increased appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes was related to the concomitant increase in gyrencephaly.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential relationship between gene emergence and brain morphology.

claim: The increased appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes in the branch leading to human may be related to the concomitant increase in brain size.
source: With regard to the branch leading to human, one may speculate whether the increased appearance of new cNPC-enriched genes was related to the concomitant increase in brain size.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential relationship between gene emergence and brain size.

claim: The majority of human-specific genes show marked differences not only in the level but also in the cNPC-type specificity of their mRNA expression compared to their ancestral paralog.
source: As to the issue of maintenance vs. modification of the cell-type specificity of expression of the human-specific genes, it is striking to observe that the majority of these genes, despite arising by entire or partial gene duplications, show marked differences not only in the level but also in the cNPC-type specificity of their mRNA expression compared to their ancestral paralog.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the expression analysis data.

claim: After gene duplication, human-specific genes underwent specific changes in regulatory elements at the transcriptional and/or post-transcriptional level during human evolution.
source: These data suggest that during human evolution, after gene duplication, these genes underwent specific changes in regulatory elements at the transcriptional and/or post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression differences between human-specific genes and their ancestral paralogs.

claim: Expressing the human-specific cNPC-enriched gene NOTCH2NL in mouse embryonic neocortex increased the abundance of cycling basal progenitors, a hallmark of the developing human neocortex.
source: Indeed, we found that expressing the human-specific cNPC-enriched gene NOTCH2NL in mouse embryonic neocortex increased the abundance of cycling basal progenitors, a hallmark of the developing human neocortex.
evidence: This is based on the in utero electroporation experiments and connects the finding to known features of human neocortical development.

claim: The NOTCH2NL protein studied is predicted to lack a signal peptide.
source: The NOTCH2NL protein studied here is predicted to lack a signal peptide
evidence: This is based on protein sequence analysis.

claim: The human-specific function of ARHGAP11B in cNPCs arose by a single-nucleotide substitution that generated a new splice donor site.
source: Moreover, we previously showed that the human-specific function of ARHGAP11B in cNPCs arose by a single-nucleotide substitution that generated a new splice donor site, the use of which generates a novel human-specific C-terminal protein sequence that we implicate in basal progenitor amplification (Florio et al., 2015; Florio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: The single-nucleotide substitution in ARHGAP11B presumably occurred relatively recently during human evolution, after the partial gene duplication event approximately 5 million years ago.
source: Importantly, this single-nucleotide substitution presumably occurred relatively recently during human evolution (Florio et al., 2016), that is, after the partial gene duplication event ~5 million years ago (Riley et al., 2002; Antonacci et al., 2014; Dennis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on evolutionary analysis from prior work.

claim: An ARHGAP11B splice variant is specifically expressed in human bRG.
source: Furthermore, we have identified here an ARHGAP11B splice variant that is specifically expressed in human bRG (Figure 8), the basal progenitor type thought to have a key role in neocortex expansion (Lui et al., 2011; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Betizeau et al., 2013; Borrell and Götz, 2014; Florio and Huttner, 2014).
evidence: This is based on splice variant analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: The bRG-specific ARHGAP11B splice variant contains only a short 3'-UTR lacking predictable microRNA binding sites, in contrast to another splice variant with a long 3'-UTR with predicted microRNA binding sites that is predominantly expressed in aRG.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the other protein-coding ARHGAP11B splice variant detected, which contains a long 3'-UTR with predicted microRNA binding sites and which is predominantly expressed in aRG, the bRG-specific ARHGAP11B splice variant contains only a short 3'-UTR lacking predictable microRNA binding sites.
evidence: This is based on splice variant analysis and microRNA binding site prediction.

claim: ARHGAP11B mRNAs may be subject to differential, microRNA-mediated, regulation depending on whether ARHGAP11B functions in the lineage progression from aRG to bRG or in bRG amplification.
source: This suggests that ARHGAP11B mRNAs may be subject to differential, microRNA-mediated, regulation depending on whether ARHGAP11B functions in the lineage progression from aRG to bRG or in bRG amplification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential 3'-UTR structure of ARHGAP11B splice variants.
